questions.question: Beta lactams.

parts.text: How do they work (4 lines allotted, 2 points)
What is the best pharmacokinetic parameter to measure them?
What’s a way of maximizing the effectiveness given (b) ?

questions.model_answer:
a) Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins and inhibit the transpeptidase step of peptidoglycan cross-linking, which triggers autolysin activity and bacterial cell lysis (bactericidal action).
b) Best parameter: time above MIC (fT>MIC) - a time-dependent pharmacodynamic index.
c) Way to maximize effectiveness: use extended/continuous infusion dosing (or more frequent dosing intervals) to prolong the time free drug concentration exceeds the MIC.

questions.question: For the following antibiotics, describe their i) capacity for inducing AmpC (strong/weak), ii) susceptibility to hydrolysis by AmpC (high/low), iii) whether they are recommended for invasive infection.

parts.text: Ceftriaxone
Cefepime
Piperacillin-tazobactam
Ceftazidime-avibactam
Imipenem

questions.model_answer:
Ceftriaxone: weak AmpC inducer; HIGH susceptibility to AmpC hydrolysis; NOT recommended for invasive infection with an AmpC-producing organism.
Cefepime: weak AmpC inducer; LOW susceptibility to AmpC hydrolysis (relatively stable); may be considered/recommended for invasive infection with an AmpC producer.
Piperacillin-tazobactam: weak-to-moderate inducer; HIGH susceptibility to hydrolysis (tazobactam does not reliably inhibit AmpC); NOT recommended for invasive infection with an AmpC producer.
Ceftazidime-avibactam: avibactam inhibits AmpC, so LOW susceptibility to hydrolysis; recommended for invasive infection with an AmpC producer.
Imipenem: strong AmpC inducer, but LOW susceptibility to hydrolysis (carbapenems are stable against AmpC); recommended for invasive infection, including with stably derepressed AmpC producers.
questions.beyond_mandell: Clinical treatment recommendations for AmpC-producing Enterobacterales reflect current IDSA guidance on resistant gram-negative infections.

questions.question: 31. Give one theoretical advantage of regimen A over regimen B based on pharmacokinetics.

parts.text: For Gram negative acute pyelonephritis: A: Gentamicin once daily, B: Gentamicin thrice daily
b) For Pseudomonas pneumonia with increased MICs, but not resistant to PIP-TAZO: A: Pip-Tazo in a continuous infusion, B: Pip-Tazo in separate doses
c) For MRSA bacteremia: A: Vancomycin thrice daily, B: Vancomycin twice daily

cohort_answer.text: Once-daily gentamicin rationale: Aminoglycoside bactericidal activity is concentration dependent - higher peak/MIC ratio gives greater rate/extent of kill; goal is to maximize drug concentration at site of infection (optimum when exposure is ~8-10x MIC). Aminoglycosides exhibit a post-antibiotic effect (PAE, 0.5-8hrs). Saturable uptake in renal tubule cell/inner ear - once daily dosing gives lower renal cortical tissue concentration than divided/continuous dosing. Adaptive resistance (first exposure effect) - down-regulation of uptake after initial exposure; longer dosing interval preserves antibacterial activity. Decreases emergence of resistant subpopulations when peak is ≥8x MIC. Continuous Pip-Tazo infusion: maintains drug levels above MIC longer (time-dependent killing), better for bugs with minimal PAE. Vancomycin TID vs BID: killing depends on 24hr AUC/MIC; more frequent dosing gives higher AUC/MIC and better killing. NB. Vancomycin is cleared renally so actual dosing depends on weight/CrCl; goal trough >15 in severe infections.

questions.question:
21. Explain the benefit of regimen (a) over regimen (b): (3)
a) Once daily dosing gentamicin vs b) Three times daily dosing gentamicin
a) PipTazo continuous infusion for Pseudomonas with elevated MIC (but still susceptible) vs b) PipTazo four times daily
a) Vancomycin three times daily for MRSA vs b) Vancomycin two times daily for MRSA

parts.text: Benefit of once daily vs three times daily gentamicin
Benefit of PipTazo continuous infusion vs four times daily
Benefit of vancomycin three times daily vs two times daily for MRSA

cohort_answer.text: Once-daily gentamicin: Higher dose gives higher concentration and post-antibiotic effect, more efficient killing; gentamicin is concentration-dependent (Cmax/MIC); PAE up to 2-6 hours in vitro, longer with higher peak; Cmax/MIC >8 correlates with less emergence of resistance; possibly lower risk of oto/nephrotoxicity. PipTazo continuous infusion: Time-dependent killing agent, greater efficacy with T>MIC; continuous infusion maintains concentrations above MIC longest, option for Pseudomonas with higher MICs. Vancomycin TID vs BID: Better area under the curve; efficacy best predicted by AUC/MIC ratio (combination of T>MIC and Peak:MIC); AUC24/MIC targets can be met with shorter interval dosing or increased dose

parts.text: 22. What are three mechanisms of resistance in Pseudomonas that would render an isolate still susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam? (3)

cohort_answer.text: Not affected by ESBL or AmpC enzymes; not affected by active efflux (upregulation of MexXY, MexAB); not appreciably affected by porin channel loss of OprD (cannot overcome MBL; not active against class A KPC, contrary to ceftaz-avi)

questions.question: Beta lactams

parts.text: Mechanism of action?
What's the main pharmacodynamic parameter that affects the action of the drug?
Given this, what is a way to administer the drug that would make it more effective?
What percentage of patients who say they have a penicillin allergy have a positive skin test?

questions.model_answer:
a) Mechanism of action: beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), inhibiting the transpeptidase (cross-linking) step of peptidoglycan cell wall synthesis, which activates autolysins and causes bacterial cell lysis (bactericidal).
b) The main pharmacodynamic parameter is time above the MIC (fT>MIC) - beta-lactams display time-dependent killing.
c) Way to maximize effectiveness: administer by extended or continuous infusion (or more frequent dosing) rather than rapid bolus, to maximize the proportion of the dosing interval that free drug concentration remains above the MIC.
d) Only about 10% of patients who report a penicillin allergy have a positive skin test (i.e., roughly 90% test negative, and true IgE-mediated allergy is uncommon).
questions.beyond_mandell: Time-above-MIC PD target and infusion strategy are established PK/PD pharmacology, and the ~10% positive skin-test figure reflects broader penicillin-allergy literature beyond this chapter excerpt.

questions.question: For gram positive pathogens name:

parts.text: 2 mechanism of beta lactam resistance
2 alternative agent and their mechanism of action

questions.model_answer:
a) Two mechanisms of beta-lactam resistance in gram-positive organisms: (1) beta-lactamase (penicillinase) production hydrolyzing the beta-lactam ring (e.g., S. aureus) (2) altered/low-affinity penicillin-binding proteins (e.g., PBP2a encoded by mecA in MRSA, altered PBPs in penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae).
b) Two alternative agents and mechanism: (1) Vancomycin - binds the D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of peptidoglycan precursors, blocking transglycosylation/transpeptidation and cell wall synthesis (2) Linezolid - binds the 23S rRNA of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit, blocking formation of the 70S initiation complex and inhibiting protein synthesis.

questions.question: Pneumococcal pneumonia with pen MIC of 2 and high MICs for clinda and eryth.

parts.text: What is the mechanism of pen resistance?
Can pen be used here?
What is mechanism of macrolide resistance?
Which mechanism in play here?

cohort_answer.text: Penicillin: Mechanism of resistance: altered enzyme structure (PBP) with reduced affinity for the antibiotic. Can be used if IV completely (MIC ≤2). If oral (or CNS infection), cannot use it. Macrolides and Clindamycin: Most likely mechanism is ermB (methylation of ribosome binding site). This gives high level resistance to macrolides and clindamycin (MLSB phenotype). Another mechanism of resistance is mefA (efflux pump), which is low level resistance, but this does not generally impact clindamycin

questions.question: Explain the benefit of regimen (a) over regimen (b) for: once daily vs three times daily gentamicin dosing; Pip-tazo continuous infusion vs four times daily for Pseudomonas with elevated MIC; Vancomycin three times daily vs two times daily for MRSA

parts.text: Once daily gentamicin vs TID dosing - benefit of once daily?
Benefit of TID gentamicin dosing over once daily?
Pip-tazo continuous infusion vs QID - benefit of continuous infusion?
Benefit of QID pip-tazo dosing?
Vancomycin TID vs BID for MRSA - benefit of TID?
Benefit of BID vancomycin dosing?

cohort_answer.text: Once daily gentamicin: convenience/adherence, less renal toxicity risk (saturable proximal tubule accumulation), concentration-dependent killing, post-antibiotic effect. TID gentamicin: can monitor trough/peak levels for PK adjustment (burns, pregnancy, renal impairment), better for synergy in endocarditis. Pip-tazo continuous infusion: time-dependent killing supports extended-infusion dosing, increasing time over MIC. Pip-tazo QID: convenience of dosing. Vancomycin TID: killing depends on AUC/MIC, allows higher AUC/MIC for maximum bactericidal effect. Vancomycin BID: convenience, adherence, less toxicity risk

questions.question: Odontogenic infection.

parts.text: Name 2 bugs not covered by amox
Name 2 bugs not covered by metronidazole
Explain why metronidazole only covers anaerobe and not aerobe

cohort_answer.text: Bugs not covered by amox: Fusobacterium (some resistance to PCN, significant resistance to clindamycin and linezolid; susceptible to Flagyl, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos and carbapenems); Prevotella (significant resistance to clindamycin; susceptible to Flagyl, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos, carbapenems, linezolid); Porphyromonas (susceptible to Flagyl and beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor combos, carbapenems, linezolid; significant resistance to clindamycin); Peptostreptococcus. Bugs not covered by metronidazole: all the aerobes - Streptococcus, Moraxella, Lactobacillus, Enterobacteriaceae. Why metronidazole only covers anaerobes: the enzyme that activates/oxidizes metronidazole (pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase / ferredoxin) is only present in anaerobic bacteria, not aerobic ones.

questions.question: Beta lactams.

parts.text: What is the mechanism of action
What PD parameter is important for these?
What is a way to administer these to take advantage of this PD parameter

questions.model_answer:
a) Mechanism of action: binding of PBPs, inhibiting peptidoglycan transpeptidase cross-linking, leading to cell wall failure and bacterial lysis.
b) Key PD parameter: time above MIC (fT>MIC) - time-dependent bactericidal activity.
c) Administration strategy: prolonged or continuous infusion to maximize time above MIC.
d) Approximately 90% of people who report a penicillin allergy will have a negative skin test.
questions.beyond_mandell: The ~90% negative skin-test figure reflects established penicillin-allergy epidemiology beyond this excerpt.

parts.text: Name 2 pharmacodynamic mechanisms which explain bacterial killing and differentiate between antibacterial classes? Give two examples of antibiotics for each pharmacodynamic mechanism.

cohort_answer.text: Concentration-Dependent Killing: Aminoglycosides, Fluoroquinolones, Daptomycin - rate/extent of killing increases with peak drug concentration; AG and FQ also have post-antibiotic effect; can be given at longer dosing intervals than predicted by half-life. Time-Dependent Killing: all beta-lactams, Clindamycin, Macrolides - free concentration maintained above MIC for a drug-specific fraction of time between doses achieves efficacy; maximizing duration of exposure (continuous infusions) leads to greater efficacy. (Alternate answer - bacteriostatic vs bactericidal: Bacteriostatic - inhibit growth/division - Tetracycline, Linezolid, Macrolides, Clindamycin. Bactericidal - kills bacteria - all beta-lactams, TMP/SMX (sometimes), Glycopeptides (weakly), Fluoroquinolones, Aminoglycosides.)

(3 - 0.5 each); Valganciclovir over acyclovir; Famciclovir over acyclovir; Doxycycline over Septra; Metronidazole over clindamycin; Piptazo over meropenem; Ampicillin over cloxacillin; cefazolin over cloxacillin; Cefuroxime over CTX; Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin; Fluconazole over caspofungin; Atovaquone over dapsone

parts.text: I would pick _____ over _____ because patient on carbamazepine
I would pick _____ over _____ because patient has G6PD deficiency
I would pick _____ over _____ because drug NOT used for C.diff treatment and NOT associated with development of C.diff
I would pick _____ over _____ because it has superior renal penetration
I would pick _____ over _____ because it works better for CMV
I would pick _____ over _____ because I need CNS coverage

questions.model_answer:
a) Because patient is on carbamazepine (a potent CYP3A4 inducer with significant drug-interaction potential with azoles): choose caspofungin over fluconazole to avoid a clinically significant CYP-mediated interaction.
b) Because patient has G6PD deficiency: choose atovaquone over dapsone (dapsone causes oxidative hemolysis in G6PD deficiency; atovaquone does not).
c) Because the drug is NOT used for C. difficile treatment and NOT associated with causing C. difficile: choose doxycycline over Septra (TMP-SMX) - doxycycline carries a low risk of precipitating C. difficile infection and is not a CDI treatment.
d) Because of superior renal/urinary penetration: choose cefazolin over cloxacillin (cefazolin achieves higher urinary concentrations; cloxacillin has substantial hepatobiliary elimination).
e) Because it works better for CMV: choose valganciclovir over acyclovir (acyclovir has minimal activity against CMV; valganciclovir/ganciclovir are the drugs of choice).
f) Because CNS coverage is needed: choose moxifloxacin over levofloxacin (moxifloxacin achieves higher CNS penetration due to greater lipophilicity).

questions.question: Q53 (2007). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. Name the resistance mechanism for each, as well as suggested treatment: Macrolides (+ explain D test); Beta-lactamases; Pseudomonas and carbapenems

parts.text: State mechanisms and treatments for each category

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides: efflux (mefA gene, lower level resistance MIC<=16); ribosomal methylation (ermB gene, high level MIC>=64). D test checks for inducible clindamycin resistance via inducible erm gene - blunting of zone of inhibition around clindamycin proximal to erythromycin disk (D-shaped zone = positive, indicates induced clindamycin resistance); suggested treatment: beta-lactam or vancomycin for GPC, septra for MRSA. Beta-lactamases: bacteria produce enzymes breaking down beta-lactam (penicillinase, cephalosporinase/ESBL, carbapenemase); treatment depends on spectrum - use cephalosporin/aztreonam/carbapenem, add beta-lactamase inhibitor, or switch classes (tigecycline, colistin). Pseudomonas and carbapenems: porin loss (OprD deficiency confers high resistance esp to imipenem); efflux pump; carbapenemase.

Options given: Acyclovir over valacyclovir; Valganciclovir over valacyclovir; Famciclovir over acyclovir; Atovaquone over dapsone; Doxycycline over TMP-SMX; Fluconazole over caspofungin; Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate; Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem; Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin; Metronidazole over clindamycin; Azithromycin over clarithromycin; Ampicillin over cloxacillin; Cefazolin over cloxacillin

parts.text: Match the drug-pair choices to the appropriate clinical scenario phrases

questions.model_answer: No specific clinical-scenario phrases were provided in this batch to match against the drug-pair list, so a specific matched answer cannot be given reliably. General rationale for each pair, for reference: Valganciclovir over valacyclovir/acyclovir - superior CMV activity. Famciclovir over acyclovir - once/twice-daily dosing, better bioavailability, similar HSV/VZV coverage. Atovaquone over dapsone - avoids hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Doxycycline over TMP-SMX - avoided in sulfa allergy, low C. difficile risk. Fluconazole over caspofungin - oral bioavailability/step-down therapy for susceptible Candida, but avoided with strong CYP3A4 interactions (e.g., carbamazepine). Liposomal amphotericin B over amphotericin deoxycholate - reduced nephrotoxicity/infusion reactions. Piperacillin-tazobactam over meropenem - carbapenem-sparing for susceptible organisms. Moxifloxacin over levofloxacin - better CNS penetration and anaerobic coverage. Metronidazole over clindamycin - lower C. difficile risk. Azithromycin over clarithromycin - fewer CYP3A4 drug interactions (e.g., in a patient on carbamazepine or other CYP3A4 substrates). Ampicillin over cloxacillin - preferred for Enterococcus. Cefazolin over cloxacillin - better tolerability/renal penetration for MSSA bacteremia.
